ACD: A brisk, assured storyteller who treats every detail as possible evidence and keeps events moving toward a solution.
Clean, well-proportioned sentences; exposition is delivered economically, and tension builds through quick exchanges and pointed reports.
Plain, educated late-Victorian English, exact about objects, clothing, hands and weather, with a gentlemanly reserve.
Talk is crisp and purposeful, each speaker sharply individuated by manner and class.
CB: Intense and passionate, giving inner feeling urgency and moral seriousness, with a fierce sense of injustice.
Vigorous sentences alternate between hard-won restraint and sudden surges of emotion.
Plain, forceful words set against vivid, sometimes Gothic imagery of weather, fire and landscape, with scripture close at hand.
Dialogue is combative and probing; characters test one another in sharp, candid exchanges.
CD: An exuberant, theatrical storyteller who moves freely between comedy, pathos and indignation and comments openly on characters.
Expansive sentences accumulate through repetition, parallel phrasing and comic elaboration.
Crowded, vivid description of streets, interiors and institutions, with fanciful comparisons that bring objects to life.
Characters are marked by distinctive idiolects, catchphrases and verbal tics, often comic.
GE: A wise, sympathetic, intellectually weighty narrator who reflects on motive and generalises about human nature.
Long, carefully qualified sentences weigh causes against consequences and trace the slow growth of feeling.
Learned and analytic vocabulary, drawing on science, history and philosophy, yet grounded in concrete provincial detail.
Characters speak in voices sharply differentiated by class and region, including rural dialect.
HGW: A clear, practical, often ironic voice with a journalist's or scientist's curiosity and an impatience with convention.
Direct, energetic sentences move quickly from observation to speculation.
Plain modern prose mixing technical and scientific vocabulary with ordinary middle-class idiom; extraordinary events reported matter-of-factly.
Talk is colloquial and lively, from comic ordinary people to earnest, argumentative idealists.
JA: Poised, ironic narration, closely attuned to characters' thoughts and slipping into their view with gentle mockery.
Elegant, balanced sentences prefer understatement to emphasis and often turn on a quiet antithesis.
An abstract vocabulary of judgement, manners, feeling and conduct, with sparse physical description.
Conversation is a contest of social position, revealing folly and good sense in what each speaker chooses to say.
JC: A brooding, morally searching voice; events are filtered through memory, interpretation and ironic distance.
Long, rhythmic sentences layered with qualification, often rendering an impression before its meaning is understood.
Dense atmospheric description of light, darkness, heat, water and silence, beside abstract moral vocabulary.
Speech is halting, oblique or formal, with foreign idioms and much left unsaid.
MS: An earnest, impassioned, confessional voice charged with sensibility and melancholy, inclined to reflect gravely on its own suffering.
Long, flowing, emotionally heightened sentences build through cumulative clauses toward anguish or exaltation.
Elevated Romantic diction; sublime landscapes, storms, solitude and ruin are described through the feelings they arouse.
Speech is eloquent and declamatory, often extended into impassioned appeals or laments.
OW: An urbane, detached voice that delights in paradox and the inversion of moral commonplaces.
Polished, balanced sentences often turn on an epigrammatic reversal; in fable, a cadenced, solemn simplicity.
Decorative aesthetic imagery of jewels, flowers, colours and fabrics, beside drawing-room elegance.
Talk sparkles with aphorism and repartee; characters say outrageous things with perfect composure.
VW: Fluid, lyrical narration moving through consciousness, rendering perception and memory moment by moment.
Sinuous sentences interrupt themselves, turn aside and pass between minds; rhythm matters more than plot.
Impressionistic imagery of light, colour, sound and passing time, with ordinary objects charged with significance.
Spoken words are sparse and fragmentary, set against the much larger life of unspoken thought.
